caption: Hasegawa et al. (2011), Supplemental Video S1. A budgerigar pecks to the audiovisual metronome.
credit: Ai Hasegawa, Kazuo Okanoya, Toshikazu Hasegawa, and Yoshimasa Seki
reference: Hasegawa, A., Okanoya, K., Hasegawa, T., & Seki, Y. (2011). Rhythmic synchronization tapping to an audio–visual metronome in budgerigars. Scientific Reports, 1, 120. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep00120
teaching: The bird was trained to peck a lit key during an acceptable window around an audiovisual stimulus. The stimulus lasted 300 ms. A successful sequence required six successive accepted pecks. Compare the timing of the peck with onset, rather than simply asking whether the animal moves repeatedly. A trained response can match a rate without every response coinciding with stimulus onset.

caption: Hattori et al. (2013), Supplemental Video_S1. A chimpanzee learns alternating keyboard taps.
credit: Yuko Hattori, Masaki Tomonaga, and Tetsuro Matsuzawa
reference: Hattori, Y., Tomonaga, M., & Matsuzawa, T. (2013). Spontaneous synchronized tapping to an auditory rhythm in a chimpanzee. Scientific Reports, 3, 1566. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep01566
teaching: Training established alternating taps on C4 and C5. Completing 30 taps produced a chime and food reward. This recording shows how a measurable repetitive motor action is established. Unlike Ronan's continuous head trajectory, keyboard contact provides discrete event times. The trained action should be distinguished from later spontaneous alignment with an irrelevant auditory rhythm.

caption: Hasegawa et al. (2011), Supplemental Video S2. A second budgerigar performs the trained tapping task.
credit: Ai Hasegawa, Kazuo Okanoya, Toshikazu Hasegawa, and Yoshimasa Seki
reference: Hasegawa, A., Okanoya, K., Hasegawa, T., & Seki, Y. (2011). Rhythmic synchronization tapping to an audio–visual metronome in budgerigars. Scientific Reports, 1, 120. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep00120
teaching: Compare the bird's discrete peck-and-reward task with the rewarded head bob in Ronan. The authors reinforced pecks within a hit window instead of rewarding movement speed alone. This second participant makes the stimulus and operant contingency visible, extending the first recording's focus on event alignment. A learned timing action is a preparation in which phase relative to the stimulus can be quantified.

caption: Hasegawa et al. (2011), Supplemental Video S3. Earlier tapping tempo persists after an interval change.
credit: Ai Hasegawa, Kazuo Okanoya, Toshikazu Hasegawa, and Yoshimasa Seki
reference: Hasegawa, A., Okanoya, K., Hasegawa, T., & Seki, Y. (2011). Rhythmic synchronization tapping to an audio–visual metronome in budgerigars. Scientific Reports, 1, 120. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep00120
teaching: At a transition to a new stimulus interval, some birds initially continued at a previously learned rate. Retention of the previous interval makes the distinction between motor period and the new stimulus period visible. Students should compare the sequence of response intervals with the changed metronome, rather than treat any repetitive pecking as successful transfer. The study identifies this recording and Video S4 as examples of interval retention.

caption: Hattori et al. (2013), Supplemental Video_S2. Ai aligns keyboard taps with a 600-ms sound sequence.
credit: Yuko Hattori, Masaki Tomonaga, and Tetsuro Matsuzawa
reference: Hattori, Y., Tomonaga, M., & Matsuzawa, T. (2013). Spontaneous synchronized tapping to an auditory rhythm in a chimpanzee. Scientific Reports, 3, 1566. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep01566
teaching: Ai aligned tapping with an irrelevant auditory sequence whose interstimulus interval was 600 ms, close to her spontaneous tapping interval. Food depended on completing the trained sequence, not on matching the distractor sound. No-sound and randomly timed controls did not show the same stable phase relation. This comparison separates a preferred motor rate from the concentration of events relative to a particular external beat, and shows why spontaneous local alignment differs from Ronan's trained broad-tempo transfer.

caption: Hasegawa et al. (2011), Supplemental Video S4. Another example of retained timing during a tempo transition.
credit: Ai Hasegawa, Kazuo Okanoya, Toshikazu Hasegawa, and Yoshimasa Seki
reference: Hasegawa, A., Okanoya, K., Hasegawa, T., & Seki, Y. (2011). Rhythmic synchronization tapping to an audio–visual metronome in budgerigars. Scientific Reports, 1, 120. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep00120
teaching: This separate recording supplies a second motor pattern during a change between trained intervals. Use it to contrast transient persistence of an old period with adjustment to a new base rate in the sea-lion tests. A previous timing pattern can carry over even when the current metronome has changed. The authors found that the 600-ms condition was retained particularly often; this is a behavioral result about temporal persistence, not a direct recording of a neural oscillator.

caption: Hattori and Tomonaga (2020), Movie S2. Sound-induced quadrupedal swaying in a chimpanzee.
reference: Hattori, Y., & Tomonaga, M. (2020). Rhythmic swaying induced by sound in chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes). Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117(2), 936–942. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1910318116
teaching: The supplementary caption identifies quadrupedal swaying. Sound playback induced rhythmic movement, but the study found no reliable relationship between horizontal swaying periodicity in this posture and the tested sound tempi. Contrast this response with the direct phase and period measurements in Ronan. Movement in the presence of rhythm, body posture, tempo adjustment, and phase matching are separate behavioral properties. This clip is useful precisely because it prevents students from treating all sound-induced movement as demonstrated beat synchronization.
